# Jose Romero · Senior Product Designer

Jose Romero is a senior product designer based in Zaragoza, Spain, with 12 years
of professional experience across digital product design, conversion rate
optimisation (CRO), behavioural economics, and design operations.
He works in English and Spanish at professional level (C1 English).

This file holds the full text of every English page on the site, one after another, so an assistant can read the whole portfolio in one request. Each page is also available on its own as markdown: request the page with Accept: text/markdown, or open /md/<path>/index.md.

# About · Jose Romero, Senior Product Designer

12 years designing digital products for banking, retail, marketplaces, hospitality and insurance. Now embedded in IKEA’s New Business Platform in Spain.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/about/

Jose Romero · Zaragoza, Spain About

# Hard problems, by choice.

I’m Jose Romero, a senior product designer with 12 years in digital products, CRO and design systems. I work in English and Spanish from Zaragoza, and I’m currently embedded in IKEA’s New Business Platform, designing two peer-to-peer marketplaces.

Before that: three years running UX and CRO for enterprise clients at Flat 101, and a design studio I co-founded in Havana.

Career

## Brands I've designed for, _across twelve years._

None of it was planned. The projects got harder, longer and fewer, until I ended up inside one product team.

Earlier Breadth 120+ Projects across disciplines: branding, print, video, digital, and campaigns Then Complexity 13 Enterprise accounts at Flat 101, across banking, insurance, hospitality, and retail Now Depth 2 Products in active design, embedded inside IKEA's product team

Skills & tools

## The skills I bring, _and the tools I use for them._

This is my own toolkit. Most of my work now runs through AI: GitHub Copilot in VS Code at IKEA, and Claude for building, prototyping and writing, alongside the design, research and experimentation tools I’ve used for years. Pick a skill to see which of my tools it draws on, or a tool to see where I use it.

### AI practice

#### AI facilitation

Turning what AI produces into material a team can read, discuss and act on. Most of my facilitation now is structuring and decoding AI output so a team can take it in without overload and act on it.

#### AI workflow design

Multi-agent workflows with hard human checkpoints, built on Shape Up. The full framework is in [Designing with AI](https://www.joseromerodesign.com/thinking/ai-workflow-framework/).

#### Context and skill building

Writing the skills, project instructions and memory that make agents work the team’s way: tone, standards, and what to check before handing anything back.

#### Agentic reporting

Reports, decks and dashboards built by agents in VS Code, connected to Jira, Confluence and Microsoft 365. It has almost replaced my office tools.

#### Designing in code

Prototypes and production UI built with AI, with Figma connected to the code. This site is one of them.

#### Knowledge systems

Research tooling that grades its own evidence. [BECO](https://www.joseromerodesign.com/thinking/beco-explorer/) links 452 behavioural-science sources to 254 concepts in a Neo4j graph.

### Design and research

#### Product design

End-to-end product design across web and mobile, from research and flows to prototypes and specs engineering can build from.

#### Experimentation and CRO

Hypotheses, A/B and multivariate tests, and results that hold up in front of stakeholders. I still run experiments in Optimizely and ContentSquare on the Second-hand Marketplace.

#### Behavioural economics

Defaults, friction, loss aversion and social proof applied to real design decisions, with BECO as the evidence behind them.

#### UX research

Moderated and unmoderated research, in-store sessions, heuristic reviews and WCAG audits, turned into direction a team can use.

#### Design operations

Ways of working across Figma, Jira, Confluence and Phrase, and the stakeholder work that keeps product, engineering and business moving, in English and Spanish.

### Tools I use

- GitHub Copilot: My main tool at IKEA: reports, decks and dashboards built with agents.

- VS Code: Where Copilot and Claude work: code, docs and reports.

- Claude: Building, prototyping and writing, with skills set up my way.

- Anarlog: Meeting notes and synthesis: my own adapted version, running on local models and connected to Copilot.

- Neo4j: The graph database behind BECO.

- Python: Data pipelines for BECO.

- Figma: Source of truth for design, now connected to code through AI.

- FigJam: Workshops and shaping sessions.

- Miro: Cross-team mapping.

- Notion: Notes, knowledge and process documentation.

- Jira: Sprint and ticket tracking, read by agents for reporting.

- Confluence: Ways-of-working docs and specs.

- Phrase: Localisation and copy management.

- Microsoft 365: Office suite, now mostly worked through agents.

- Optimizely: A/B and multivariate testing.

- ContentSquare: Behavioural analytics and experiment analysis.

- Hotjar: Session recordings and heatmaps.

- Google Analytics: Traffic and funnel measurement.

- AB Tasty: Experimentation and personalisation.

- VWO: Conversion testing.

- Optimal Workshop: Card sorting and tree testing.

# Thinking · Jose Romero, Senior Product Designer

How I approach design work: on strategic empathy, behavioural economics, systems that survive people, and what it means to design with AI in the room.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/thinking/

Things I've thought about long enough to put into words, drawn from 12 years across enterprise product, CRO and team leadership.

**1 essay**·**1 research project**·**4 positions**, updated October 2026

## Essays and _research._

A framework built from real work, and BECO, a research project you can read about or explore.

Featured

### Designing with AI demands process design first. _Tool choice second._

A full framework for human-led, agent-assisted product design: three-tier agent architecture, genuine checkpoints, the drift problem, and what this shift demands from senior designers.

18 min read · AI · Process Design → Research · BECO

### A knowledge graph that grades its own evidence. _Visual walkthrough._

A personal, DOI-verified graph of 450+ behavioural-science sources, built to separate what the research actually shows from what design decks have been repeating for a decade.

Visual explainer · AI · Behavioural Science → Research · BECO · Interactive

### The whole graph on one map. _With a card for every point._

All 254 concepts, the findings and sources behind them and the people who wrote those sources, on one map you can zoom through. Beside it, a card reads whatever you pick, with every study cited and how well it backs the concept.

Interactive · AI · Behavioural Science →

## Shorter _positions._

Short takes on how I work. Open one to read it.

There's a version of empathy that's emotional: you put yourself in someone's position and feel what they might feel. That has real value: it's the foundation of personal connection and deep user trust. But in design work, especially inside large organisations, what's more useful day-to-day is a different kind: the ability to map how another person understands the situation, what they're optimising for, what they're afraid of, and what they need to be true in order to move forward.

I've started calling this positional empathy. It sits alongside compassion rather than standing in for it, and it's turned out to be one of the more useful skills I've picked up in enterprise work. Most of the genuinely hard problems in these environments have nothing to do with visuals or technical execution. People show up misaligned, working from different mental models of the same problem, carrying incentives the brief never mentions.

Map that out accurately, without losing your own read on it, and you can usually work through it. The goal is to understand the situation well enough that people stop arguing about the wrong things.

> You map stakeholder alignment the same way you'd map any other system.

The standard design process asks what users need. That's a fine question, but it's not the one I spend most of my time on. The behavioural economics question asks something narrower and, I'd argue, more useful: given how people's cognition actually works, with its shortcuts and biases and context-dependence, what is this specific interface going to make them do?

Years of conversion rate optimisation across banking, insurance, loyalty, and e-commerce taught me that the answer to that question usually comes down to details nobody thinks to argue about: the order information appears on a page, whether a choice is framed as a gain or a loss, whether there's a default option at all. Get those wrong and no amount of good intentions in the brief saves the design.

The point is to understand how decisions are actually made, under time pressure, with incomplete information, shaped by context, and designing for that reality rather than an idealised version of it.

> What users need and what users do are different questions. The behavioural approach changes the choice architecture itself instead of collecting more stated preferences.

When I joined the IKEA Home Services team, there was no shared working system. Files existed everywhere. The hierarchy of work, what belonged in Figma, what in Confluence, what in Jira, was unclear and inconsistently applied. The process that existed depended on specific individuals to hold it in memory and transmit it informally. When those individuals weren't available, the system collapsed.

My approach was to start with principles rather than tools. I mapped the actual work the team was doing: the types of tasks, their interdependencies, the decisions that kept getting lost. From that, I derived a set of structural rules, what goes where, when, and why, that could be documented, taught, and modified without requiring me to be present.

Adoption was messy, honestly, but the underlying structure held up regardless. That's what I was aiming for: a process solid enough to keep working when people don't follow it to the letter. It's already outlived changes in the team, a round of new hires, and the stretches where nobody had time to babysit it. That's the real test, and it passed.

> A good system keeps working when people don't follow it perfectly.

What I've been exploring over the past year is what happens when you introduce AI into a design process that was already complex, specifically, the Shape Up methodology my team uses at IKEA. Shape Up asks people to hold a lot of context, make judgment calls on incomplete information, and move quickly through shaping decisions that have long downstream consequences.

AI can process and produce information faster than any team can absorb it. Which means the bottleneck shifts. The work moves from generating options to making sense of them: having enough shared context to evaluate what the AI has produced and decide what to do with it.

The hard part turned out to be human: getting an AI-assisted process to produce output that's actually useful instead of just plentiful, building in checkpoints at the moments that actually need human judgment, and keeping a room full of people from getting buried in AI-generated text and losing track of the decision they were actually there to make.

All of that is facilitation work. Which, it turns out, is design work too.

> AI moves where judgment is needed. The bottleneck shifts from generation to sense-making, and structuring that process is a design problem.

[Read the full framework →](https://www.joseromerodesign.com/thinking/ai-workflow-framework/)

These positions will change. The work continues.

# IKEA Home Services · Jose Romero

Designing IKEA’s peer-to-peer home improvement marketplace from concept to launch in seven Spanish regions. 500,000+ downloads, 4.9/5 satisfaction.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/ikea-home-services/

Product Design · Marketplace · Mobile

# Peer-to-peer home improvement marketplace.

Connecting homeowners with verified local professionals across 50+ home improvement categories, designed from early concept through to a live product now running across seven Spanish regions.

- **Client:** IKEA / Ingka Group

- **Agency:** Garaje de Ideas / Groupe EDG

- **My role:** Senior Product Designer (Implant)

- **Period:** 2025–Present

- **Scope:** Product Design · UX Research · Mobile · Accessibility

## In short

The problem

IKEA wanted a marketplace for home services that earned the trust of homeowners and professionals at the same time, inside a brand that’s careful about every detail.

What I did

Embedded full-time in IKEA’s product team, I designed both sides of the marketplace, ran research sessions inside IKEA stores, and built accessibility in from the first flow.

Result

Live in seven Spanish regions since its Madrid launch in 2024: 500,000+ downloads, 21,000 completed service requests and a 4.9/5 satisfaction rating, per Ingka Group.

Context

## Extending IKEA beyond furniture

IKEA's New Business Platform is an internal startup unit within Ingka Group, tasked with expanding the brand into adjacent markets across Europe. The ambition was clear: if you've just bought a flat-pack wardrobe, you probably need someone to help you put it up. And IKEA wanted to be the one to connect you.

IKEA Home Services is the result: a peer-to-peer marketplace connecting homeowners with vetted, reviewed professionals across more than 50 home improvement and assembly categories. It launched in Madrid in September 2024, reached Barcelona a year later, and expanded to seven Spanish regions by May 2026, including renovation services added in March 2026.

_Both sides of the marketplace must be convinced simultaneously: IKEA's platform acts as the trust layer that makes quality, pricing, and safety legible to both homeowners and professionals._

_**Two sides, one platform.** AI-assisted matching turns a homeowner's natural-language request into a structured job (left), while a verified onboarding flow brings professionals onto the supply side (right)._

The challenge

## Trust, consistency, and speed

Marketplace products live or die on trust. Homeowners need to trust the professionals they're letting into their homes. Professionals need to trust that the platform is worth their time. And IKEA needs the product to feel like IKEA: considered, reliable, without friction.

The additional complexity: we were building a new product inside a very large, brand-sensitive organisation, working with multiple stakeholders across product, service design, engineering, content, and the in-store IKEA network. Decisions had to be made at pace, but they had to hold up to scrutiny. The brief was never fully stable.

Trust, made explicit

Rather than leaving credibility implicit, IKEA's commitment is stated plainly at the point of decision: verified professionals, backed by the brand, with recourse if something goes wrong.

My role

## Embedded, end-to-end

I joined IKEA's New Business Platform as a Senior Product Designer embedded full-time on Home Services, working inside the product team with product owners, service designers, engineers, content designers and business developers. Today the platform runs Home Services and the Second-hand Marketplace as one team, and I still support Home Services from there.

My work spans user flows, interaction design, high-fidelity prototyping, in-store user research sessions at IKEA locations, accessibility auditing (WCAG compliance), and design handoff. I contribute to product decisions, not just design delivery.

_Embedded design means being present at every stage: from research sessions inside IKEA stores to product decisions in sprint reviews._

Approach

## Research first, iteration always

We ran user research sessions inside IKEA stores: recruiting participants on-site and testing flows in context, with the app running on real devices. This gave us faster signal than remote testing and was consistent with the product's natural discovery channel.

The design process was iterative by necessity. A marketplace has two distinct user types, homeowners and service professionals, each with different mental models and success criteria. We mapped flows for both sides separately before working on the points of intersection: booking, confirmation, dispute resolution, and review mechanics.

Accessibility was treated as a requirement from day one, not an audit at the end. The product had to meet IKEA's own accessibility standards alongside WCAG AA, across iOS and Android.

_**Discovery.** Search by need, browse the services within a category, and review a verified professional's profile. Each step builds confidence before the homeowner commits to anything._

_**The booking moment.** IKEA Family sign-in as step one ties the request to the wider ecosystem, a considered loading state keeps the user oriented, and a confirmation that sets expectations clearly closes the loop._

Outcomes

## Strong adoption from launch

500k+ Downloads 21k Service requests completed 57k New or reactivated IKEA Family members 4.9 Customer satisfaction rating

These are published figures from Ingka Group. The product launched in Madrid in September 2024 and has since expanded to seven Spanish regions as of May 2026, with continued growth in progress.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Run the research inside IKEA stores

Why

Recruiting on site and testing flows on real devices gave faster signal than remote testing, and matched how people find the product anyway.

### Map the two sides separately, then design where they meet

Why

Homeowners and professionals have different mental models and different ideas of success. Each side's flows came first; booking, confirmation, dispute resolution and review mechanics came after.

### Treat accessibility as a requirement from the first flow

Why

The product had to meet IKEA's own accessibility standards and WCAG AA across iOS and Android, so it was a requirement from day one rather than an audit at the end.

Learnings

## What building inside a large brand teaches you

Being embedded inside IKEA's team has confirmed something for me: the design itself is rarely the hard part. Keeping a coherent direction while stakeholder priorities shift, the roadmap moves, and people rotate on and off the team. That's the actual job. Fighting that instability is a losing battle. Building systems that can absorb it isn't.

This project also sharpened how I think about trust in a marketplace. Visual polish and a smooth onboarding flow barely register next to things like how a professional's credentials get displayed, what happens on screen when a booking goes wrong, or the exact wording of a review prompt. Nobody labels those as "design decisions," but that's exactly what they are, and they carry most of the weight.


---

# IKEA Second-hand Marketplace · Jose Romero

Peer-to-peer resale of IKEA products using IKEA's own catalogue as a listing backbone. Piloted in Spain, now live in five European countries.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/ikea-secondhand-marketplace/

Product Design · Marketplace · Circular Commerce

# IKEA‑native resale, at European scale.

A peer-to-peer marketplace for buying and selling used IKEA products, with IKEA's own catalogue acting as a structural backbone for listings. Piloted in Spain and Norway, now live across five European countries.

- **Client:** IKEA / Ingka Group

- **Agency:** Garaje de Ideas / Groupe EDG

- **My role:** Senior Product Designer (Implant)

- **Period:** 2025–Present

- **Scope:** Product Design · Cross-functional · Multi-market

## In short

The problem

A pilot in Madrid and Oslo had to grow into one product that works across markets with different payment systems, consumer laws and second-hand habits.

What I did

I designed the listing, trust and review flows to stay consistent across markets, and worked with engineering on how IKEA’s own catalogue fills in each listing automatically.

Result

Live in five countries (Spain, Norway, Portugal, Poland and Sweden), with Ingka aiming for around 170,000 listings in 2026. Commercial figures aren’t public yet.

Context

## Circular commerce built on IKEA's own catalogue

IKEA's sustainability commitments require more than recycling materials; they require rethinking the lifetime of the product. A second-hand marketplace solves that problem commercially: it keeps IKEA products in circulation, creates value for sellers, and lowers the barrier to buying IKEA for price-conscious buyers.

What makes this product structurally interesting is its data backbone. Because IKEA's product catalogue is exhaustive and machine-readable, listings don't need manual product descriptions: the platform can retrieve dimensions, materials, assembly instructions, and compatibility data automatically from the IKEA database. This dramatically reduces listing friction and increases trust.

_IKEA's product catalogue acts as the structural backbone: removing listing friction for sellers while delivering verified product identity and secure payment to buyers._

The challenge

## Scaling a pilot across markets

The product launched as a pilot in Madrid and Oslo in August 2024, running in parallel with IKEA Home Services inside the same New Business Platform. As the pilots proved themselves, the pressure shifted: from getting the product to work in one market to making it work across five, with different payment systems, different consumer protection laws, and different levels of second-hand market maturity.

This meant the design work had to be modular. Assumptions valid in Spain couldn't be hardcoded into components that would serve Norway or Portugal. Localisation wasn't an afterthought; it was a structural constraint from the beginning of the expansion phase.

_From two pilot cities in 2024 to five markets in early 2026: each expansion phase stress-tested localisation assumptions before the next rollout._

My role

## Product design across the full lifecycle

I started on the Second-hand Marketplace as a collaborator, while my main work was Home Services. Today one New Business Platform team runs both products, and the Second-hand Marketplace is where most of my work goes: product design, cross-functional collaboration, and the shared design operations framework that supports both products.

As the platform has matured and scaled, the nature of the work has shifted from defining new flows to refining and extending a system that needs to remain coherent across markets and team changes.

Approach

## Modular by design

Working across two marketplace products has a useful side effect: patterns that work in one tend to inform the other, and design debt in one becomes visible faster when you're maintaining consistency across both. The listing creation flow, the trust and safety messaging, the review architecture: these were developed with cross-product consistency in mind.

The IKEA catalogue integration required close collaboration with engineering to define the data contract between the catalogue and the UI. What fields were always available? What fields were optional or inconsistently populated? The answers shaped the information hierarchy of every listing page.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Design for modularity once the product expanded

Why

Assumptions that held in Spain could not be hardcoded into components that would serve Norway or Portugal, where payment systems, consumer law and second-hand habits differ.

Result

Each expansion phase stress-tested the localisation assumptions before the next rollout.

### Let the catalogue data contract set the listing hierarchy

Why

Working with engineering, we listed which fields the IKEA catalogue always provides and which arrive optional or patchy. Those answers decided the information hierarchy of every listing page.

Result

Sellers do not write product descriptions; dimensions, materials and assembly data come from the catalogue.

### Build listing, trust and review flows for both marketplaces at once

Why

A pattern that works in one product tends to inform the other, and design debt in one shows up faster when you keep both consistent.

Status

## Live in five markets, scaling further

The platform launched as a pilot in Madrid and Oslo in August 2024. Through 2025 it expanded to Spain, Norway, Portugal, and Poland. Sweden joined in January 2026, bringing the total to five active markets. Ingka Group has committed to continuing EU-wide expansion, with a target of approximately 170,000 listings in 2026. Specific commercial performance figures are not published publicly at this time.

# Santander Nordics CRO Programme · Jose Romero

Lead UX/CRO designer on conversion optimisation for loan, credit card and deposit funnels in Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/santander-nordics-cro/

CRO · Banking · Multi-market

# Data-driven optimisation across four markets.

Lead UX/CRO designer on an ongoing programme of conversion optimisation across consumer loan, credit card, deposit, and car loan funnels in Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and Norway.

- **Client:** Santander Consumer Finance Nordics

- **Agency:** Flat 101

- **My role:** Lead UX / CRO Designer

- **Period:** 2022–2025

- **Markets:** Denmark · Sweden · Finland · Norway

## In short

The problem

Raise conversion on loan, card and deposit funnels in four Nordic markets, where every change needs legal sign-off and a false result costs more than in e-commerce.

What I did

For three years I led UX and CRO design: structured hypotheses, variants across the whole funnel with a focus on application forms, QA on live tests, and results explained to four in-market teams.

Result

The application form was rebuilt test by test and became the default in all four markets. A change only shipped after significant uplifts in at least the two largest, so no win rested on one market, culture or season.

Context

## CRO inside a regulated banking environment

Santander Consumer Finance operates consumer lending across multiple European markets. In the Nordics (Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and Norway) they offer consumer loans, credit cards, deposit products, and car financing through dedicated digital funnels, each localised to its market.

The CRO programme at Flat 101 was an ongoing retainer engagement: continuous hypothesis generation, experiment design, test execution, and results analysis. My role was lead UX/CRO designer, responsible for the design side of the experimentation process, working alongside analysts, developers, and Santander's in-market digital teams.

The challenge

## Precision in a constrained environment

Banking is one of the most regulated digital environments you can work in. Every change to a funnel page goes through legal review. Certain UI patterns (urgency messaging, social proof, framing) require explicit sign-off. The scope for experimentation is narrower than in e-commerce, and the cost of a false result is higher.

Working across four markets means juggling four sets of constraints at once. Something legally fine in Denmark can be restricted in Norway. Copy that resonates with Swedish users can fall flat in Finland. Localisation here meant regulatory review and cultural read, not just translation.

Approach

## Hypothesis-first, data-rigorous

Every experiment began with a structured hypothesis: a specific behaviour we observed or predicted, a proposed intervention, a measurable outcome, and a defined significance threshold. This discipline keeps experimentation honest, and in a regulated environment, it also provides the paper trail required for stakeholder sign-off.

The design work covered the full funnel: landing pages, product comparison pages, application forms, confirmation flows, and re-engagement touchpoints. Application forms (the highest-stakes, highest-drop-off stage) were a consistent focus. The behavioural economics principles most relevant here: reducing perceived effort, managing anxiety around sensitive financial information, using progress indicators and milestone framing to maintain commitment.

I was also responsible for communicating results clearly to Santander's teams across four markets: translating statistical results into actionable design direction and translating stakeholder feedback into testable hypotheses.

The work was structured around a three-pillar approach: deep analytics and session data to surface friction, heuristic and behavioural economics evaluation to understand why that friction exists, and disciplined hypothesis development to prioritise interventions by potential impact. The team operated on a structured sprint cadence with a dedicated Kanban board tracking each experiment from backlog through to live. Beyond designing variants, I maintained QA oversight on test implementations, validating that live variants matched approved specifications before results were collected. In a regulated environment where a misconfigured test produces misleading data, implementation fidelity is as much a design responsibility as the variant itself.

Control Variant A

**Consumer loan funnel · Step 2:** Restructured field grouping and progress framing to reduce perceived effort at the highest drop-off point in the application flow.

_Each experiment moves through the same seven-stage cycle. Legal Review is the regulatory gate: sign-off is required across all four Nordic markets before any variant goes live. The loop closes at Learn, where every result, including failures, updates the hypothesis library and informs the next sprint._

Control Variant OP2

**Insurance info page:** Reordered trust signals and simplified pricing presentation. Regulated content constraints required legal sign-off across all four markets before the variant could go live.

Control Variant

**Insurance add-on nudge:** Behavioural nudge applied at the insurance decision point in the loan funnel. Timing and framing derived from anxiety-reduction and commitment heuristics.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Keep returning to the application form

Why

It was the highest-stakes step and the one where most people dropped off, so a gain there counted for more than one on a landing page.

Result

The form was rebuilt test by test, and the winning version became the default in all four markets.

### Ship only on a significant uplift in the two largest markets

Why

So that no result rested on one market, one culture or one season. The method we agreed with Santander was stricter than on most projects.

Cost

A win in a single market stayed a test result and did not go live.

Result

What reached the live funnels had held up in more than one market.

### Check every live test against the approved spec

Why

Every variant needed legal sign-off in four markets, and a misconfigured test produces misleading data. Implementation fidelity is as much a design responsibility as the variant itself.

Result

Results were collected only from variants that matched what had been approved.

Learnings

## What multi-market CRO teaches you about design

Working across four markets simultaneously sharpens your understanding of what's universal and what's contextual in design. Some friction points appear consistently regardless of market: long form fields without inline validation, ambiguous progress indicators, unclear error messages. Others are deeply market-specific.

CRO work also teaches you to hold your own taste loosely. A design looking good and a design performing well line up often enough to be dangerous, you start assuming they're the same thing. When the data disagrees with your instinct, the data wins, every time.

**What I can share about the results:** the application form was redesigned over time from the experiments that won, and that version became the default in all four markets. A change only shipped once it showed a significant uplift in at least the two largest markets, so that no result depended on a single market or on cultural or seasonal effects. Banking in regulated markets is sensitive enough that the methodology we agreed with Santander was stricter than on most projects. The exact figures stay under NDA.

# Meliá Hotels · Campaign Management Platform · Jose Romero

An internal campaign management platform for Meliá Hotels: from director workshops to live in under a year, then refined over three across all markets.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/melia-hotels-campaign-platform/

Product Design · Web Application · Hospitality

# A platform built from zero, live in twelve months.

Conceptualised, designed, and optimised a marketing campaign management platform from scratch for Meliá Hotels International, from multi-department workshops with senior directors to a fully launched internal tool managing campaigns across all Meliá markets.

- **Client:** Meliá Hotels International

- **Agency:** Flat 101

- **My role:** Lead Product Designer

- **Duration:** 2022–2025

- **Scope:** Product Design · Facilitation · Internal Tool

## In short

The problem

Meliá ran campaigns across more than 40 countries on email threads and spreadsheets. Nothing existed to replace them, so the requirements had to come from the people doing the work.

What I did

As lead product designer I ran workshops with senior directors, mapped how a campaign really moves from idea to review, and designed the platform’s architecture, interactions and handover documentation.

Result

Live in under twelve months and refined for two more years, it now runs campaigns across all Meliá markets in place of the spreadsheet-and-email system. Figures are commercially sensitive.

Campaign Hub / Development / Media Plan Campaign Hub / Development overview Context

## A large hospitality group with a coordination problem

Meliá Hotels International is one of Europe's largest hotel groups, with properties across more than 40 countries and a complex international marketing structure. Managing campaign activity across brands, markets, and departments relied on a combination of email threads, spreadsheets, and manual coordination, a system that worked until the volume of concurrent campaigns made it fragile.

The brief was to design an internal platform that gave Meliá's marketing teams a single place to create, review, approve, schedule, and track campaigns across their global portfolio. This was a zero-to-one product problem: nothing existed, and the requirements had to be discovered, not specified.

Discovery

## Director-level workshops, across departments

The engagement began with a structured discovery phase: multi-hour workshops with senior directors from multiple international departments at Meliá's headquarters. These weren't standard stakeholder interviews. They were working sessions designed to surface the mental models and workflow assumptions of people who had been managing campaigns manually for years.

The tricky part of this phase is that people rarely describe what they need. They describe the solution they've already pictured in their head. Senior stakeholders especially: ask what they want and you get a product spec, not a problem statement. My job was to listen to that spec, then work backward to the actual problem underneath it.

"Asking 'what do you want' gets you a wish list. Asking 'show me what breaks' gets you an actual project."

From those sessions, we derived a shared model of how campaigns actually moved through the organisation: from idea to brief, brief to asset, asset to approval, approval to scheduling, scheduling to performance review. Each stage had different owners, different blockers, and different information needs.

_Discovery to live in under twelve months, then two further years of refinement, and a platform that kept evolving after the engagement ended. The brief was a blank page; the requirement was that it outlast us._

**Minimum times framework.** A strategic artefact I built from scratch based on deep knowledge of the campaign process, mapping the minimum lead time required per phase and development module. This became the architectural backbone every campaign setup was validated against.

Design & delivery

## Live in a year, refined over three

The platform went from first workshop to live in under twelve months, a timeline that required moving fast from discovery through architecture to a functioning product. The engagement then ran for a further two years of ongoing refinement and improvement, with the platform continuing to evolve even after my involvement ended. My role throughout was lead product designer, responsible for the UX architecture, interaction design, design system consistency, and the ongoing working relationship with Meliá's internal teams.

The platform evolved significantly from its initial design. Early testing revealed two distinct groups with fundamentally different needs: campaign creators who just needed to move fast without extra steps in the way, and marketing managers who needed visibility and control instead. This led to approval gateways, a visual campaign timeline view, and reporting dashboards, none of which were in the original brief, all of which emerged directly from user behaviour. The interface shifted from a content-management model toward a workflow-first structure: organised around campaign states, handoff actions, and role-based views tailored to each team.

Working with a rotating engineering team across the engagement also taught me a great deal about design-to-development handoff. Consistency in component naming, documentation of interaction states, and explicit specification of edge cases, the unglamorous work of design systems, became increasingly important as the team changed and institutional knowledge had to live in the documentation, not in people's heads. The engagement concluded with a structured handover: documentation, training sessions for the Meliá team, and a role-based access model that ensured each user type had the tools and interface they needed to manage and evolve the platform independently.

**User permissions matrix.** One of two reference documents I designed to specify access logic across 8 roles and 15 platform sections, used directly by engineers as the source of truth for backend permission configuration and frontend conditional rendering.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Ask "show me what breaks", not "what do you want"

Why

Senior stakeholders describe the solution they have already pictured. Asking what breaks gets a problem statement you can design for.

Result

The workshops produced a shared model of how a campaign moves: idea, brief, asset, approval, scheduling, performance review.

### Build a minimum-times framework as the architecture's backbone

Why

It maps the minimum lead time each phase and module needs, drawn from deep knowledge of the campaign process.

Result

Every campaign setup was validated against it.

### Split the product by role after early testing

Why

Testing showed two groups with different needs: creators who wanted to move fast, and marketing managers who wanted visibility and control.

Result

Approval gateways, a visual campaign timeline and reporting dashboards, none of them in the original brief. The interface moved from content management to a workflow-first structure.

Outcome

## Live across all Meliá markets

The platform launched and is in active use across Meliá's international operations, managing live campaigns across all of the group's markets. It replaced the fragmented spreadsheet-and-email system that preceded it.

The specific performance numbers here are commercially sensitive, so I can't share them. What I can say is that a product that started life as a blank brief, shaped through workshops, launched inside a year, and refined over three more, is now in daily use, at scale, by the teams it was actually built for.

# Mapfre · Digital Expansion · Jose Romero

Lead product designer on Mapfre Internacional’s expansion: Verti in Italy and Germany, an office directory for Latin America, and a CRO programme.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/mapfre-digital-expansion/

Product Design · Multi-market · Design System

# Multi-market platform design, at the design lead level.

Lead product designer on Mapfre Internacional's digital platform work: Verti brand redesign across Italy and Germany, an Insurance Offices & Agents Directory deployed across Latin America, and a CRO programme for international digital properties. All in English, across multiple markets and a shared development partner.

- **Client:** Mapfre Internacional

- **Agency:** Flat 101

- **My role:** Lead Product Designer

- **Period:** 2023 – 2025

- **Scope:** Platform Design · Design System · Multi-market

## In short

The problem

Verti’s sites in Italy and Germany had grown apart over years, mostly by accident, while Mapfre Internacional also needed a directory for Latin America and a CRO programme, all with one development partner.

What I did

I led design across three programmes: supervising two designers on the Verti redesigns built on Mapfre’s design system, designing the offices and agents directory, and shaping the experiments for the CRO work.

Result

Verti Italia and Germany now share one design system with Verti’s branding intact, and the directory went live in Brazil, Peru and Nicaragua. The CRO work found the data too immature to test reliably, so it narrowed to where results could be measured.

verti.it Context

## A separate account, a different kind of complexity

The Mapfre engagement at Flat 101 covered two legally distinct entities. Mapfre España, which included the AFIN financial app, operated independently from Mapfre Internacional, which managed the Verti direct insurance brand across European markets and digital properties across international territories. Both accounts ran in parallel at Flat 101, but with entirely different client teams, technical stacks, and design needs.

The Internacional work was conducted entirely in English, with Capgemini as the shared development partner across all programmes. Complexity wasn't just about the number of markets; it was about managing multi-agency delivery across teams that each operated under different organisational cultures and timelines.

Verti · Platform redesign

## Two markets, one convergence approach

Verti is Mapfre's direct insurance brand, operating in Italy, Germany, and Spain. The platforms had evolved independently per market, accumulating inconsistencies in UX patterns, design system components, and conversion flows. Some differences were intentional (regulatory or cultural requirements), but most were simply the result of independent development without shared standards.

The engagement began with Verti Italia: a full platform redesign migrating from a custom-built platform to the Mapfre corporate design system, while preserving Verti's distinct branding and adapting to Italian regulatory requirements. Verti Germany followed as a sequential project: same methodology, same design system foundation, applied to Germany-specific requirements, brand criteria, and technical constraints. My role on both was design lead, directly supervising two designers throughout the engagement. Daily responsibilities included client requirements alignment, progress presentations with the Mapfre and Capgemini teams, work plan definition and phase management, and maintaining coherence between the Mapfre corporate system and Verti's own branding.

_Three markets that had evolved independently. The design work was convergence: audit to separate intentional divergence from accidental drift, then a shared design system as the foundation. One component library, three localized market surfaces._

Approach

## Shared structure, localized surface

Before any redesign, most of the audit work was figuring out which cross-market differences were actually intentional (regulatory requirements, local conventions, deliberate brand calls) and which had just accumulated because each market had built independently for years with no shared standard to check against. Those two categories needed completely different fixes, and mixing them up would have meant either breaking something a market needed or preserving an accident as if it were policy.

The shared design system became the operational foundation: components, interaction patterns, and conversion flows consistent across markets, defined once and adapted at the surface layer. For a brand like Verti, which has its own strong branding within the Mapfre family, this required careful work at the boundary between the Mapfre corporate system and Verti's own aesthetic. The goal was not uniformity; it was coherence without flattening the brand.

preventivo.verti.it · La tua polizza auto

**Verti Italia, Self-service funnel.** The first step of the prospecting flow, redesigned as part of the Verti platform convergence: policy type, vehicle details, and CTA in a single, uncluttered entry point.

Offices & Agents Directory

## A public-facing feature for international markets

Alongside the Verti platform work, I designed a public-facing product feature for Mapfre Internacional: an Insurance Offices & Agents Directory enabling users to find nearby Mapfre offices and registered insurance agents. The feature comprised three interconnected components: an interactive map, a filterable directory listing, and individual profile pages per office and per agent.

Initial deployment covered Brazil, Peru, and Nicaragua, with a structured rollout to additional markets underway at the point of handover. Multi-market deployment required careful consideration of localisation beyond language: address format conventions, map provider integration per territory, regulatory requirements for displaying licensed agent information in each country, and country-specific page structures for local compliance.

mapfre.com.br · Oficinas Referenciadas

**Insurance Offices Directory, Brazil.** Interactive map with clustered markers across São Paulo. Filterable directory, office listings, and individual agent profile pages, deployed across Brazil, Peru, and Nicaragua.

_Three concurrent workstreams, one client, one agency, one development partner. Each programme required its own rhythm and team configuration, all managed from the design lead role._

CRO Programme

## Experiment design for international properties

A conversion rate optimisation programme ran alongside the platform redesign work, applying structured hypothesis development and experiment design to Mapfre Internacional's digital properties. The work covered the full CRO pipeline: data analysis to surface friction points, hypothesis formulation, design of test variants, implementation specification, and results analysis.

**What the CRO work found:** the teams were too isolated from each other, and data across products wasn’t mature enough to support proper experimentation. We narrowed the scope to smaller, more mature parts of the process, where results could be attributed and reach statistical significance on a realistic timeline. That surfaced refactoring work that had to happen before testing was possible, so the programme didn’t get far while I was on it.

Design leadership

## Running three programmes from the lead role

Running concurrent programmes for the same client required clear workload management across the team. For the Verti work specifically, leading two designers meant defining task scope and priorities, reviewing output quality and brand coherence, and handling all client-facing presentations and requirements alignment. Work plans, phase definitions, and effort estimates were mine to define and maintain.

Daily communication with the Mapfre teams and Capgemini in English, across multiple markets and time zones, required documentation and status management rigorous enough that all parties stayed aligned without constant synchronisation. In a multi-agency environment, the cost of miscommunication lands on the design team first, and fast feedback loops between design, development, and client are the only effective mitigation.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Separate intentional divergence from accidental drift before redesigning

Why

Some differences between markets were regulatory or cultural; most had piled up because each market built on its own. The two need different fixes, and mixing them up either breaks something a market needs or preserves an accident as policy.

Result

Verti Italy and Germany now share one design system with Verti's branding intact.

### Aim for coherence, not uniformity

Why

Verti has a strong brand inside the Mapfre family, so the work at the boundary between the corporate system and Verti's own look had to be careful.

Result

Components, patterns and flows are defined once and adapted at the surface layer.

### Narrow the CRO scope to what could be measured

Why

The teams were isolated from each other and the data across products was not mature enough for proper experiments. Smaller, more mature parts of the process could reach significance on a realistic timeline.

Cost

The scope got smaller.

Result

It surfaced refactoring that had to happen before testing was possible, so the programme did not get far while I was on it.

Learnings

## What multi-market platform work teaches you

The most useful distinction in multi-market design is between divergence that serves the user and divergence that serves no one. Platforms that evolve independently tend to accumulate a lot of the second kind: inconsistencies that developed because nobody was watching, not because the local market required them. Finding and removing that accidental drift is its own design discipline, and it's usually where the biggest efficiency gains are sitting, waiting for someone to notice them.

Leading design across several concurrent programmes, each with its own team, timeline, and level of client readiness, taught me something about what the lead role is actually for. Quality control is the easy part. The harder part is keeping one coherent picture of the whole engagement in your head when every individual programme has a natural pull toward becoming its own silo.

Specific performance data for this engagement is subject to NDA.

# Mapfre · AFIN Financial App · Jose Romero

Lead UX designer on AFIN, Mapfre’s self-service finance app: progressive disclosure, and a Financial Advisor built on trust and transparent data use.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/mapfre-afin-digital-expansion/

Product Design · FinTech · Mobile & Web

# Self-service finance, designed for trust.

Lead UX designer for AFIN, Mapfre's self-service financial management app covering investments, savings, and pension plans, from progressive disclosure information architecture to a new Financial Advisor feature built around personalised guidance, transparent data collection, and preserved user autonomy.

- **Client:** Mapfre

- **Agency:** Flat 101

- **My role:** Lead UX / Product Designer

- **Period:** Dec 2022 – Aug 2023

- **Scope:** Product Design · Mobile & Web · FinTech

## In short

The problem

Mapfre wanted to add a Financial Advisor to its savings and investment app, which meant asking people about money and risk without losing their trust or the app’s simplicity.

What I did

As lead UX designer I rebuilt the app around progressive disclosure, designed a data-collection flow that explains every question, and showed the reasoning behind each recommendation. I also led the move from Sketch to Figma.

Result

The redesign wasn’t built at the time for lack of resources and priority, but it became the baseline other designers used to improve parts of the app. The move to Figma sped up backlog work and made collaboration easier for everyone.

afin.mapfre.es · simulación a futuro Context

## A self-service financial app at a complex intersection

AFIN is Mapfre's self-service financial app for individual customers, covering savings products, investment portfolios, and pension plans. The product sits at an intersection that's rare in financial services: it needs to feel simple enough for customers who aren't financially sophisticated, while being trustworthy enough for customers making long-term financial decisions.

That tension between simplicity and completeness is really the central design challenge in financial app UX. Strip too much away and customers lose information they actually need; show everything and you overwhelm the person who just wanted a quick status check. Most of the actual design work here was finding the right balance at every layer of the product, not just once at the top.

The challenge

## Adding a Financial Advisor without breaking trust

The primary objective of the engagement was introducing a Financial Advisor feature: a personalised guidance system generating product recommendations based on each user's risk profile and financial goals. A meaningful new capability, and a correspondingly complex design problem.

Three problems ended up shaping most of the work. Fitting a substantial new feature into an app that already had its own information model, without breaking that coherence, was the first. The second was getting people to actually trust a data-collection flow that asks about their financial situation, risk appetite, and long-term goals. Most financial apps never earn that level of transparency. The third was the recommendation engine itself: push too hard and it reads as a sales tool, which kills trust faster than not recommending anything at all, so every suggestion had to visibly show its reasoning.

_Four layers, three product types. The default view loads fast with what most users need most of the time. Every additional layer, detail then action, is one deliberate tap deeper. Complexity on demand, not by default._

Approach

## Progressive disclosure, not progressive complexity

The engagement opened with a discovery phase: customer journey mapping across multiple user entry points to understand how different users moved through the app, what they came for, where they dropped off, and where the information architecture was creating unnecessary friction. That research shaped the layered model the redesign was built around.

The UX architecture was built around progressive disclosure: the default view presents the summary most users need most of the time, with a consistent path to detail available at every level. No feature is hidden, but not every feature needs to be prominent. The Financial Advisor sits at the deepest layer of this hierarchy: always available, never intrusive.

Financial product UX also requires careful attention to the language of trust. How you label a product (pension plan vs. retirement savings), how you present performance data, how you communicate risk: these are design decisions with real consequences for the decisions users make. I worked closely with Mapfre's product and legal teams to define language conventions that would hold across the whole product.

_Four layers, three product types. The default view loads what most users need most of the time. Each additional layer, detail then action, is one deliberate tap deeper. Complexity on demand, not by default._

The Financial Advisor

## Personalised guidance, with visible reasoning

The advisory feature required designing a data collection flow that users would willingly complete. Asking someone about their financial risk tolerance and long-term goals is sensitive: the design had to communicate clearly why the information was being collected and how it would be used, without burying that context in legal language. Each question was framed in plain terms with transparent purpose.

The recommendation output had to earn trust at the point of display: every suggested product was shown with its rationale, why this product, why now, what assumption it was based on. Users could accept a recommendation, modify the inputs that generated it, or ignore it entirely. Preserving that autonomy, making the guidance feel like informed advice rather than a sales funnel, was the defining design constraint of the feature.

_The advisory flow is designed around trust at every step. Data collection is transparent and purposeful. Recommendations are shown with visible reasoning. User autonomy is preserved throughout; the system advises, it does not decide._

_**Advisory flow, mobile**: entry point, investment proposal with risk controls, and signed confirmation. Three steps from a single user journey._

Design decision

When a user tries to leave the advisory flow mid-process, the exit modal intercepts with a callback offer: "We'll call you." Abandonment becomes a route into assisted help rather than a lost session. A small decision with measurable retention implications.

Design operations

## Migration, coordination, and handoff

The engagement included a significant design operations challenge from the outset: the app had an extensive screen library and complete design system built in Sketch, requiring full migration to Figma while active feature development continued in parallel. I planned and led that migration, defining the structure, phases, and effort estimates, ensuring no disruption to ongoing product work throughout.

Coordination with Capgemini, the development partner, was a constant throughout: disciplined handoff and regular multi-team alignment were essential across design, client, and engineering teams operating under different organisational structures. The multi-device scope (desktop, tablet, and mobile) added a further layer of specification and handoff complexity to every delivery.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Layer the app with progressive disclosure

Why

The app had to feel simple for customers who are not financially sophisticated and still hold up for long-term decisions. The default view carries what most people need most of the time; detail and action are one deliberate tap deeper.

Result

The Financial Advisor sits at the deepest layer: always available, never intrusive.

### Show the reasoning behind every recommendation

Why

Pushing too hard reads as a sales tool, and that costs more trust than not recommending at all.

Result

Each suggested product came with why this product, why now and what assumption sat behind it. Users could accept it, change the inputs or ignore it.

### Offer a callback when someone tries to leave the advisory flow

Why

Leaving the advisory flow mid-way used to mean a lost session. A "We'll call you" offer turns the exit into a route to assisted help.

Learnings

## What financial UX teaches you about trust

Financial products make the stakes of UX decisions visible in a way that consumer apps often don't. A confusing navigation pattern on a streaming service costs a user a few seconds. A confusing navigation pattern on an investment account can contribute to a decision made without sufficient information, with real financial consequences.

That reality sharpens design decisions fast, and it only works with a real working relationship with compliance and legal rather than an adversarial one. On the teams I've seen do this well, legal has learned enough about the page to accept that a required disclosure doesn't have to sit in the most disruptive spot, and design has accepted that the disclosure isn't going away regardless.

**What happened next:** AFIN had already launched to Mapfre’s finance clients before I joined, and those who opted in were using it. My redesign wasn’t implemented at the time because of resources and priorities, but it became the baseline for gradually improving specific parts of the app, work that other designers took over when I moved to other high-level projects. The process side paid off straight away: with the product designed in the cloud, on a clear structure and process instead of legacy tools, the team worked through its backlogs faster, and collaboration between stakeholders, engineers and designers improved across the board.


---

# IQOS Club Spain · CRO Programme · Jose Romero

Project lead on ongoing CRO for the IQOS Club loyalty portal: fast experiments on limited traffic, with behavioural economics applied to habit and retention.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/iqos-club-cro/

CRO · Loyalty · Behavioural Economics

# Optimising loyalty under tight constraints.

Project lead for ongoing conversion optimisation across the IQOS Club members' portal: fast-cycle experimentation, behavioural economics applied to habit and retention mechanics, operating under limited traffic and shared resources.

- **Client:** Philip Morris International (IQOS)

- **Agency:** Flat 101

- **My role:** CRO Project Lead

- **Period:** 2022–2025

- **Scope:** CRO · Loyalty · Behavioural Strategy

## In short

The problem

Grow engagement and retention in the IQOS Club members’ portal in Spain, with low traffic from existing members only, tight marketing restrictions and shared development resources.

What I did

As CRO project lead I built the experiment pipeline, from analytics and heuristic review to hypotheses ranked by impact and cost, designed the variants and personalisation in VWO, and set the programme’s direction with the client.

Result

Engagement improved across the programme, which ran for the whole engagement, and the client came to use VWO as a fast channel for launch campaigns. Specific figures are confidential.

Control iqosclub.es Variant 6 iqosclub.es Context

## A loyalty programme with a specific kind of complexity

IQOS Club is Philip Morris International's loyalty programme for IQOS users in Spain, a members' portal where users track rewards, access exclusive content, manage their devices, and engage with the brand between purchases. The programme sits in the tobacco alternatives category, which carries significant marketing restrictions and shapes what's possible in digital promotion.

Acquisition wasn't really the CRO challenge here. Engagement and retention were: getting existing members to use the platform more, move up through loyalty tiers, and stay connected to the brand over the long haul. That calls for a different set of levers than a standard transactional funnel.

The challenge

## Low traffic, high standards

Loyalty portals are structurally harder to optimise than transactional funnels. Traffic volumes are lower, because you're targeting only existing members, not the broader market. This means experiments take longer to reach statistical significance, and the risk of acting on false positives is higher.

In this environment, good CRO practice requires more discipline, not less. The hypothesis quality has to be higher because you can run fewer experiments. The design decisions have to be better informed because you have less data to course-correct with.

Approach

## Behavioural economics in a loyalty context

The most relevant behavioural frameworks for loyalty are different from those that dominate conversion optimisation in e-commerce. Loss aversion still applies: the framing of tier status and expiring points is a powerful lever. But habit formation mechanics become more important here: variable reward schedules, completion mechanics, progress visualisation.

As project lead, I was responsible for generating the experiment pipeline: identifying opportunity areas through analytics and heuristic review, structuring hypotheses, prioritising based on potential impact and implementation cost, and communicating the programme's direction to the client. The design work included experiment variant design, interaction specifications, and performance analysis.

The experiment pipeline ran in three phases: insight generation (web analytics, heatmaps, heuristic review, and behavioural economics framing), hypothesis and prioritisation (structuring focused hypotheses ranked by impact versus implementation cost), and rapid experimentation using Visual Website Optimizer (VWO). VWO enabled both A/B tests and personalisation variants without heavy development overhead, a key constraint given the shared-resource model. Personalisation complemented A/B work: tailoring content and mechanics to member segments, rather than forcing a single optimised experience on a heterogeneous membership base.

"In loyalty work, 'will people convert' is the easy question. The one that actually matters is whether you're building a habit or just catching them in a good mood."

Control iqosclub.es Variant 6 iqosclub.es

**Homepage: Referral programme entry point.** V6 replaced the default hero with a full-bleed lifestyle photo tied to the active referral campaign, making the referral CTA the primary visual focus. Hypothesis: a contextually relevant, campaign-led hero outperforms the default brand hero at driving referral programme engagement.

_The behavioural lever depends on the loyalty goal. CRO tests optimise the continuous hook loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, rather than isolated touchpoints._

Control iqosclub.es · Recomienda Variant 1 iqosclub.es · Recomienda

**Recomienda: Reward framing test.** The control offered 1,000 points buried in a cluttered layout. V1 reduced the reward to 500 points but redesigned the page with cleaner hierarchy and a more prominent CTA, testing whether a better-framed lower reward could outperform a higher reward presented poorly.

_Experiments run in a three-phase cycle. Insight quality feeds hypothesis quality; hypothesis quality determines how much learning can be extracted from limited traffic._

Case 1 · 2,500+ pts iqosclub.es Case 5 · <500 pts iqosclub.es

**Personalisation: Segment-led homepage CTA.** Members with 2,500+ points see a "Canjear puntos" primary CTA, the natural next step for a high-balance member. Members below 500 points see earn-oriented CTAs with a teal notification bar surfacing relevant actions. Same hero; different primary intent.

Outcome

## Ongoing programme with measurable engagement gains

The IQOS Club engagement improved across the programme period. Specific figures are subject to client confidentiality and have not been published. The programme ran continuously throughout the Flat 101 engagement.

The more durable outcome for me was methodological: running CRO at low traffic volumes sharpens your thinking about what makes a good hypothesis and what constitutes meaningful evidence. The discipline of making high-quality decisions with limited data is transferable to almost any design context.

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Raise the quality of each hypothesis instead of running more tests

Why

Only existing members visit the portal, so experiments take longer to reach significance and a false positive is more likely to be acted on. With fewer experiments possible, each one has to be better argued.

Cost

Fewer experiments could run.

Result

A pipeline that ranked hypotheses by impact against implementation cost, built on analytics, heatmaps and heuristic review.

### Run variants in VWO so nothing waited for a development sprint

Why

Development resources were shared with other work, and VWO could run both A/B tests and personalisation without heavy engineering.

Result

The client came to use VWO as a fast channel for launch campaigns, with modals live within hours of a product launch.

### Personalise by segment instead of optimising one experience

Why

The membership base is heterogeneous, and the alternative was forcing one optimised experience on all of it.

Result

Members with 2,500+ points see a redeem call to action; those under 500 see earn-oriented ones. Same hero, different primary intent.

Scope evolution

## CRO tooling as a campaign delivery channel

As the programme matured, something useful happened: the client began recognising VWO not just as a testing tool, but as a fast deployment channel for time-sensitive campaign assets. Because VWO variants could go live without a development sprint, it became the preferred path for promotional modals, campaign banners, and temporary content tied to specific launches.

This was a natural evolution. The same infrastructure that let us test UX hypotheses could push a promotional overlay to logged-in members within hours of a product launch, without touching the underlying platform. Promotional modals for device releases and loyalty campaigns became a recurring deliverable alongside the A/B pipeline.

**Promotional modal: IQOS ILUMA Stardrift launch.** One of several campaign modals deployed via VWO during the programme. Triggered on login for targeted member segments, timed to product availability windows. Designed, built, and deployed without a development sprint.

# XTI Store · E-commerce Redesign · Jose Romero

A full redesign of XTI’s fashion e-commerce platform, balancing brand ambition with a Magento migration, informed by competitor analysis and Hotjar data.

Source: https://www.joseromerodesign.com/work/xti-ecommerce-redesign/

E-commerce · UI Design · Fashion

# Brand ambition within platform constraints.

Full redesign of XTI's national fashion e-commerce platform, balancing brand ambition against the real constraints of a Magento migration and informed by competitive analysis, information architecture testing, and Hotjar behavioural data.

- **Client:** XTI Store

- **Agency:** Flat 101

- **My role:** Lead UX/UI Designer

- **Period:** 2022–2025

- **Scope:** E-commerce Redesign · IA · UI Design

## In short

The problem

Redesign XTI’s fashion e-commerce site during a migration to Magento, so every design decision had to fit what the platform could actually deliver.

What I did

As lead UX/UI designer I used Hotjar data, a competitor study and card sorting and tree testing to set the structure, then redesigned the product listing and detail pages with the developers involved from the start.

Result

Launched on Magento and stayed XTI’s main store for about three years, until the brand’s next relaunch. Designed in a single month, on standard templates and a reduced budget.

xtistore.com/calzado-mujer Context

## A national fashion retailer migrating platforms

XTI is a Spanish footwear and fashion brand with a national retail presence and a significant direct-to-consumer digital operation. The redesign was scoped to coincide with a platform migration to Magento, which meant the design work had to operate within the constraints of what Magento could deliver, not an ideal technical canvas.

People underrate how much the platform itself decides the UX before you've made a single design choice. Its component model, its URL structure, its filtering logic all draw the boundaries of what's even possible, whether anyone notices or not. Knowing those boundaries going in is the difference between a design that's exciting on screen and one that actually ships.

Research & discovery

## Behavioural data first

The discovery phase used Hotjar session recordings, heatmaps, and funnel analytics from the existing site, alongside a structured competitive analysis studying how fashion category leaders like Zara and Adidas handled navigation, filtering, and product presentation. The goal was to understand where XTI's existing experience was losing users and why, before proposing any changes.

Information architecture testing was also part of the process: card sorting and tree testing exercises conducted in Optimal Workshop to validate the proposed category and navigation structure before committing to high-fidelity design. IA problems discovered in testing are much cheaper to fix than IA problems discovered in live user data, especially on a Magento migration where structural changes post-launch carry significant development cost.

_**Product listing · mobile scroll**: category hero, filter chips and grid density, mid-page editorial break. Three screens from a single scroll._

_Constraints mapped first. Research inputs are filtered through the platform constraint, and the design brief becomes: what is the best possible UX within what can actually be built?_

Design

## Balancing brand and conversion

Fashion e-commerce has a tension most other sectors don't deal with in quite the same way. The brand side wants editorial presence and a sense of aspiration; the conversion side wants clarity, product imagery front and center, and as little friction as possible between browsing and buying. Good fashion sites manage both, but only by being deliberate about exactly where brand gets to take up space and where it has to step back.

For XTI, the design decisions focused on the product listing page and product detail page, the two highest-traffic, highest-drop-off stages in any fashion funnel. Filtering and sorting UX, product image presentation, size selection, and the add-to-cart interaction were all redesigned with conversion data as the primary success measure.

The creative direction took cues from fashion editorial: clean layouts, generous whitespace, typography-led hierarchy, and product photography given room to breathe. That register was achievable within Magento's constraints because it relies on restraint rather than technical complexity. Developer collaboration was embedded from the start: involving the technical team early meant understanding what would perform within Magento's template model and avoiding patterns that would require expensive custom development.

_**Product detail · mobile scroll**: product hero and ATC, size and colour selection, similar products and reviews. The highest drop-off point in the funnel._

_The redesign concentrated effort on the highest drop-off stages: product listing and product detail. Brand expression earns its space at the top of the funnel; conversion mechanics take over from the listing page down._

Decisions

## Three decisions that shaped the work

### Map the platform's constraints before designing anything

Why

Magento's component model, URL structure and filtering logic set the boundaries of the UX before any design choice is made. Knowing them first rules out the elegant solution that cannot be built.

Result

The brief became: what is the best UX we can build on this platform?

### Test the information architecture before high-fidelity design

Why

Problems found in card sorting and tree testing are far cheaper than problems found in live data, especially on a migration where structural changes after launch carry development cost.

Result

The category and navigation structure was validated in Optimal Workshop before any high-fidelity screens.

### Concentrate the effort on the listing and product detail pages

Why

They are the highest-traffic, highest-drop-off stages of a fashion funnel. Brand expression earns its space at the top; conversion mechanics take over from the listing page down.

Result

The store launched on Magento and stayed XTI's main store for about three years.

Learnings

## Platform constraints are a design brief, not an obstacle

The experience of designing within a specific platform constraint, knowing what's possible and what isn't before starting, is valuable in a way that isn't obvious until you've done it. It eliminates a large category of wasted design work: the elegant solution that can't be built, the interaction pattern that the platform doesn't support.

It also changes what question you're actually answering as a designer. Not "what's the ideal UX here," in the abstract, but "what's the best UX I can build given what this platform will actually let me do", a less flattering question, but the one that matters when the project has to ship.

**What happened next:** the redesign launched and stayed XTI’s main store for about three years, until the brand relaunched with a new version. For the team, it was a lesson in building a distinctive, appealing store out of steep constraints: standard Magento templates without premium features, a reduced budget, and a single month to deliver the design to a high standard with few production resources.
